# Page: Sequence and Structure Data

# Sequence and Structure Data

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [src/chainreader2.cpp](src/chainreader2.cpp)
- [src/chainreader2.h](src/chainreader2.h)
- [src/cif.cpp](src/cif.cpp)
- [src/convert.cpp](src/convert.cpp)
- [src/msta_scores.cpp](src/msta_scores.cpp)
- [src/pdbchain.cpp](src/pdbchain.cpp)
- [src/pdbchain.h](src/pdbchain.h)
- [src/seqdb.cpp](src/seqdb.cpp)
- [src/seqdb.h](src/seqdb.h)

</details>



This document covers the core data structures and I/O systems for managing protein sequences and 3D structural data in reseek. The system provides unified access to multiple structural biology file formats through a set of classes that handle sequence data, coordinate information, and format conversions.

For information about database search and alignment algorithms that operate on these data structures, see [Database Search System](#4). For details about the format conversion command-line interface, see [Format Conversion System](#5.1).

## Core Data Structures

The reseek system uses three primary classes to manage sequence and structural data:

### PDBChain Class

`PDBChain` represents a single protein chain containing both sequence and structural information:

| Member | Type | Purpose |
|--------|------|---------|
| `m_Label` | `string` | Chain identifier/label |
| `m_Seq` | `string` | Amino acid sequence |
| `m_Xs`, `m_Ys`, `m_Zs` | `vector<float>` | 3D coordinates (Å) |
| `m_Idx` | `uint` | Global chain index |
| `m_Lines` | `vector<string>` | Original file lines (optional) |

Key methods include coordinate access (`GetXYZ`, `GetDist`), transformations (`Reverse`, `Flip`, `GetXFormChain_tR`), and format I/O (`ToPDB`, `ToCal`, `ToFasta`, `FromPDBLines`).

### SeqDB Class

`SeqDB` manages collections of sequences with optional alignment information:

| Member | Type | Purpose |
|--------|------|---------|
| `m_Labels` | `vector<string>` | Sequence identifiers |
| `m_Seqs` | `vector<string>` | Sequence data |
| `m_LabelToIndex` | `map<string, uint>` | Fast label lookup |
| `m_IsAligned` | `bool` | Whether sequences are aligned |
| `m_ColCount` | `uint` | Column count for alignments |

The class supports sequence addition (`AddSeq`), retrieval (`GetSeq`, `GetSeqByLabel`), and FASTA I/O (`FromFasta`, `FromFasta_Seqs`).

### ChainReader2 Class

`ChainReader2` provides universal access to multiple file formats through a state machine architecture:

```mermaid
graph TD
    STATE_Closed["STATE_Closed"]
    STATE_PendingFile["STATE_PendingFile"] 
    STATE_ReadingCALFile["STATE_ReadingCALFile"]
    STATE_ReadingBCAFile["STATE_ReadingBCAFile"]
    STATE_ReadingPDBFile["STATE_ReadingPDBFile"]
    STATE_ReadingCIFFile["STATE_ReadingCIFFile"]
    
    STATE_Closed --> STATE_PendingFile
    STATE_PendingFile --> STATE_ReadingCALFile
    STATE_PendingFile --> STATE_ReadingBCAFile
    STATE_PendingFile --> STATE_ReadingPDBFile
    STATE_PendingFile --> STATE_ReadingCIFFile
    STATE_ReadingCALFile --> STATE_PendingFile
    STATE_ReadingBCAFile --> STATE_PendingFile
    STATE_ReadingPDBFile --> STATE_PendingFile
    STATE_ReadingCIFFile --> STATE_PendingFile
```

Sources: [src/chainreader2.h:12-20](), [src/chainreader2.cpp:116-184]()

## Format Support and Data Flow

The system supports multiple structural biology file formats with automatic format detection:

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph Input["Input Formats"]
        PDB["PDB Files<br/>(.pdb, .ent)"]
        CIF["CIF Files<br/>(.cif, .mmcif)"]
        CAL["CAL Files<br/>(.cal)"]
        BCA["BCA Files<br/>(.bca)"]
        FASTA["FASTA Files<br/>(.fasta)"]
    end
    
    subgraph Processing["Processing Layer"]
        ChainReader2["ChainReader2<br/>Universal Parser"]
        PDBChain["PDBChain<br/>Data Structure"]
        SeqDB["SeqDB<br/>Collection Manager"]
    end
    
    subgraph Output["Output Formats"]
        OutPDB["PDB Output<br/>ToPDB()"]
        OutCAL["CAL Output<br/>ToCal()"]
        OutFASTA["FASTA Output<br/>ToFasta()"]
        OutBCA["BCA Output<br/>WriteChain()"]
        MultiPDB["MultiPDB<br/>MODEL Records"]
    end
    
    PDB --> ChainReader2
    CIF --> ChainReader2
    CAL --> ChainReader2
    BCA --> ChainReader2
    FASTA --> SeqDB
    
    ChainReader2 --> PDBChain
    PDBChain --> SeqDB
    
    PDBChain --> OutPDB
    PDBChain --> OutCAL
    PDBChain --> OutFASTA
    PDBChain --> OutBCA
    PDBChain --> MultiPDB
```

Sources: [src/chainreader2.cpp:49-88](), [src/pdbchain.h:46-57](), [src/seqdb.h:51-52]()

### Format-Specific Processing

Each format has dedicated parsing methods:

| Format | Detection | Parser Method | Key Features |
|--------|-----------|---------------|--------------|
| PDB | `.pdb`, `.ent` extensions | `GetFirst_PDB()`, `GetNext_PDB()` | ATOM records, chain IDs |
| CIF | `.cif`, `.mmcif` extensions | `GetFirst_CIF()`, `GetNext_CIF()` | Loop structures, field mapping |
| CAL | `.cal` extension | `GetFirst_CAL()`, `GetNext_CAL()` | Tab-delimited coordinates |
| BCA | `.bca` extension | `GetFirst_BCA()`, `GetNext_BCA()` | Binary coordinate format |

Sources: [src/chainreader2.cpp:71-86](), [src/cif.cpp:133-309](), [src/chainreader2.cpp:224-287]()

## Coordinate Systems and Transformations

### Integer Coordinate Compression

`PDBChain` uses a compressed coordinate system for efficient storage:

- Coordinates are stored as 16-bit unsigned integers
- Conversion: `CoordToIC(X) = (X + 1000) * 10 + 0.5`
- Reverse: `ICToCoord(IC) = IC/10.0 - 1000.0`
- Range: -1000.0 to +5553.5 Å

```mermaid
graph TD
    FloatCoords["Float Coordinates<br/>m_Xs, m_Ys, m_Zs"]
    IntegerCoords["Integer Coordinates<br/>uint16_t ICs"]
    
    FloatCoords -->|"CoordToIC()"| IntegerCoords
    IntegerCoords -->|"ICToCoord()"| FloatCoords
    
    FloatCoords --> GetICs["GetICs()<br/>Compress to ICs"]
    IntegerCoords --> CoordsFromICs["CoordsFromICs()<br/>Decompress from ICs"]
```

Sources: [src/pdbchain.cpp:42-68](), [src/pdbchain.h:89-90](), [src/pdbchain.cpp:423-471]()

### Geometric Operations

The system provides various geometric operations:

- Distance calculation: `GetDist()`, `GetDist2()`
- Coordinate transformations: `GetXFormChain_tR()` 
- Structural manipulations: `Reverse()`, `Flip()`
- Point operations: `GetPt()`, `SetPt()`, `GetXYZ()`

Sources: [src/pdbchain.cpp:310-497]()

## Multi-threaded Processing Pipeline

The `convert.cpp` system demonstrates multi-threaded processing of structural data:

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph MainThread["Main Thread"]
        PDBFileScanner["PDBFileScanner<br/>File Discovery"]
        ThreadManager["Thread Manager<br/>spawn/join threads"]
    end
    
    subgraph WorkerThreads["Worker Threads"]
        ChainReader2_T1["ChainReader2<br/>Thread 1"]
        ChainReader2_T2["ChainReader2<br/>Thread 2"]
        ChainReader2_TN["ChainReader2<br/>Thread N"]
    end
    
    subgraph SharedResources["Shared Resources"]
        StatsMutex["s_LockStats<br/>Progress Tracking"]
        OutputMutex["s_LockCal/s_LockFasta<br/>Output Synchronization"]
        BCAMutex["s_LockBCA<br/>Binary Output"]
    end
    
    subgraph OutputFiles["Output Files"]
        CalFile["CAL File<br/>s_fCal"]
        FastaFile["FASTA File<br/>s_fFasta"]
        BCAFile["BCA File<br/>s_ptrBCA"]
        MultiPDBFile["MultiPDB File<br/>s_fMultiPDB"]
    end
    
    PDBFileScanner --> ThreadManager
    ThreadManager --> ChainReader2_T1
    ThreadManager --> ChainReader2_T2
    ThreadManager --> ChainReader2_TN
    
    ChainReader2_T1 --> StatsMutex
    ChainReader2_T2 --> StatsMutex
    ChainReader2_TN --> StatsMutex
    
    ChainReader2_T1 --> OutputMutex
    ChainReader2_T2 --> OutputMutex
    ChainReader2_TN --> OutputMutex
    
    OutputMutex --> CalFile
    OutputMutex --> FastaFile
    BCAMutex --> BCAFile
    OutputMutex --> MultiPDBFile
```

Sources: [src/convert.cpp:74-246](), [src/convert.cpp:315-325]()

## Integration with Analysis Systems

The data structures integrate with reseek's analysis systems:

### DALI Scoring Integration

`DALIScorer` uses these structures for structural comparison:

- `LoadChains()` loads `PDBChain` objects from files
- `SetMSA()` processes `SeqDB` multiple sequence alignments
- Calculates Z-scores and LDDT metrics for structural similarity

Sources: [src/msta_scores.cpp:16-17](), [src/msta_scores.cpp:65-70]()

### Feature Extraction

The system supports feature extraction for structure analysis:

- Secondary structure prediction
- Density calculations  
- Conformational features
- Distance-based features

Feature alphabets are converted to sequence-like representations using `GetFeatureChar()` and output via `ToFeatureFasta()`.

Sources: [src/pdbchain.cpp:70-81](), [src/pdbchain.cpp:110-125](), [src/convert.cpp:185-203]()

## Memory Management and Performance

### Object Lifecycle

- `PDBChain` objects are dynamically allocated and must be explicitly deleted
- `SeqDB` manages vector storage automatically
- `ChainReader2` maintains file handles and buffers

### Thread Safety

- Global counters use `m_CRGlobalLock` for synchronization
- Per-thread locks (`m_CRPerThreadLock`) protect individual readers
- Output operations use format-specific mutexes

Sources: [src/chainreader2.cpp:97-111](), [src/convert.cpp:25-32]()

# Command-Line Interface

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

This document provides an overview of the reseek command-line interface architecture, including command dispatch, parameter processing, and output formatting systems. For detailed listings of all available commands and parameters, see [Commands and Options](#6.1). For information about customizable output columns and formats, see [Output Formatting](#6.2).

## Overview

The reseek command-line interface provides a comprehensive system for protein structure search, alignment, and format conversion operations. The CLI is built around a command-dispatch architecture where users specify a primary command followed by various options and parameters. The system supports 69 distinct commands and over 217 configuration parameters, making it highly flexible for diverse bioinformatics workflows.

## Command Architecture

The CLI system is organized around a two-level hierarchy: primary commands that determine the operation type, and options that configure the behavior of those commands.

```mermaid
graph TB
    CLI["reseek CLI Entry Point"]
    
    subgraph "Primary Commands"
        SEARCH["-search<br/>Database Search & Alignment"]
        CONVERT["-convert<br/>Format Conversion"]
        ALIGNPAIR["-alignpair<br/>Pairwise Alignment"]
        OTHER["Other Commands<br/>69 total in cmds.h"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Option Categories"
        STR_OPT["String Options<br/>Input/Output Files"]
        UNS_OPT["Unsigned Options<br/>Numeric Parameters"]
        FLT_OPT["Float Options<br/>Scoring Parameters"]
        FLAG_OPT["Boolean Flags<br/>Mode Switches"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Core Systems"
        MYOPTS["myopts.h<br/>Option Definitions"]
        CMDS["cmds.h<br/>Command Registry"]
        USAGE["usage.h<br/>Help System"]
    end
    
    CLI --> SEARCH
    CLI --> CONVERT
    CLI --> ALIGNPAIR
    CLI --> OTHER
    
    SEARCH --> STR_OPT
    SEARCH --> UNS_OPT
    SEARCH --> FLT_OPT
    SEARCH --> FLAG_OPT
    
    STR_OPT --> MYOPTS
    UNS_OPT --> MYOPTS
    FLT_OPT --> MYOPTS
    FLAG_OPT --> MYOPTS
    
    OTHER --> CMDS
    USAGE --> CLI
```

**Command Dispatch System**

The command system uses a macro-based approach to define available commands. Each command is registered in `cmds.h` using the `C()` macro, which generates the necessary dispatch table entries.

Sources: [src/cmds.h:1-78](), [src/myopts.h:1-150](), [src/usage.h:1-90]()

## Parameter Processing System

The parameter system uses a sophisticated macro-based approach to handle different types of command-line options with type safety and automatic help generation.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Option Type Macros"
        STR["STR_OPT<br/>String Parameters"]
        UNS["UNS_OPT<br/>Unsigned Integer Parameters"]
        FLT["FLT_OPT<br/>Floating Point Parameters"]
        FLAG["FLAG_OPT<br/>Boolean Flags"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Parameter Categories"
        IO_PARAMS["I/O Parameters<br/>-input, -output, -db, -fasta"]
        ALGO_PARAMS["Algorithm Parameters<br/>-threads, -evalue, -gapopen"]
        MODE_PARAMS["Mode Parameters<br/>-fast, -sensitive, -verysensitive"]
        DEBUG_PARAMS["Debug Parameters<br/>-verbose, -log, -trace_*"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Processing Pipeline"
        PARSE["Option Parsing"]
        VALIDATE["Parameter Validation"]
        DISPATCH["Command Dispatch"]
    end
    
    STR --> IO_PARAMS
    UNS --> ALGO_PARAMS
    FLT --> ALGO_PARAMS
    FLAG --> MODE_PARAMS
    FLAG --> DEBUG_PARAMS
    
    IO_PARAMS --> PARSE
    ALGO_PARAMS --> PARSE
    MODE_PARAMS --> PARSE
    DEBUG_PARAMS --> PARSE
    
    PARSE --> VALIDATE
    VALIDATE --> DISPATCH
```

**Option Definition System**

The options are defined using four primary macros in `myopts.h`:
- `STR_OPT()` for string parameters like file paths and labels
- `UNS_OPT()` for unsigned integer parameters like thread counts and sizes
- `FLT_OPT()` for floating-point parameters like scoring weights and thresholds
- `FLAG_OPT()` for boolean flags that enable/disable features

Sources: [src/myopts.h:8-64](), [src/myopts.h:66-96](), [src/myopts.h:98-116](), [src/myopts.h:117-145]()

## Output Formatting Architecture

The CLI provides a flexible output formatting system through the UserField mechanism, allowing users to customize which columns appear in their results.

```mermaid
graph TB

    end

        TSV["TSV Format<br/>Tabular Output"]
```

**Field Processing Pipeline**

The output system converts internal alignment results into user-specified output formats through the `DSSAligner::WriteUserField()` method, which handles formatting and value conversion for each field type.

Sources: [src/userfields.cpp:45-151](), [src/userfieldnames.h:1-34]()

## Usage Patterns

The CLI supports three primary usage patterns, each optimized for different bioinformatics workflows:

| Usage Pattern | Command | Primary Purpose | Key Options |
|---------------|---------|-----------------|-------------|
| Database Search | `-search` | Search query structures against a database | `-db`, `-output`, `-evalue`, `-threads` |
| Format Conversion | `-convert` | Convert between file formats | `-cal`, `-bca`, `-fasta` |
| Pairwise Alignment | `-alignpair` | Align and superpose two structures | `-input2`, `-aln`, `-output` |

**Algorithm Mode Selection**

All search operations require specifying an algorithm mode that balances speed versus sensitivity:

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Algorithm Modes"
        FAST["-fast<br/>High Speed<br/>Lower Sensitivity"]
        SENSITIVE["-sensitive<br/>Balanced<br/>Default Mode"]
        VERYSENSITIVE["-verysensitive<br/>High Sensitivity<br/>Lower Speed"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Parameter Effects"
        FILTERING["Filtering Thresholds"]
        SCORING["Scoring Parameters"]
        SEARCH_DEPTH["Search Depth"]
    end
    
    FAST --> FILTERING
    SENSITIVE --> FILTERING
    VERYSENSITIVE --> FILTERING
    
    FILTERING --> SCORING
    SCORING --> SEARCH_DEPTH
```

**Input Format Support**

The system supports multiple input formats through a unified interface:

| Format | Extension | Description | Use Case |
|--------|-----------|-------------|----------|
| PDB | `.pdb` | Legacy PDB format | Small datasets, compatibility |
| mmCIF | `.cif`, `.mmcif` | Modern PDB format | Large structures, complete metadata |
| CAL | `.cal` | C-alpha text format | Custom preprocessing |
| BCA | `.bca` | Binary C-alpha format | Large databases, performance |
| Directory | (none) | Directory traversal | Batch processing |

Sources: [src/usage.h:2-89](), [README.md:15-92]()

## Help and Documentation System

The CLI includes a comprehensive help system that provides usage information, parameter descriptions, and example commands. The help text is generated from the same macro definitions used for option processing, ensuring consistency between the implementation and documentation.

Sources: [src/usage.h:2-89](), [README.md:15-92]()

## Option Type System

```mermaid

        UNS_WINDOW["--window<br/>Window Size"]

    end

        FLT_GAPOPEN["--gapopen<br/>Gap Open Penalty"]
        FLT_GAPEXT["--gapext<br/>Gap Extension Penalty"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Boolean Flags (FLAG_OPT)"

        FLAG_FAST["--fast<br/>Fast Mode"]
        FLAG_VERBOSE["--verbose<br/>Verbose Output"]
        FLAG_QUIET["--quiet<br/>Quiet Mode"]
    end
```

**Sources:** [src/myopts.h:8-144]()

## Core Configuration Options

### Algorithm Mode Selection

The algorithm behavior is controlled through mutually exclusive mode flags that configure the entire processing pipeline:

| Flag | Purpose | Impact |
|------|---------|---------|
| `--fast` | High-speed mode | Reduced sensitivity, faster execution |
| `--sensitive` | Balanced mode | Default sensitivity/speed tradeoff |
| `--verysensitive` | High-accuracy mode | Maximum sensitivity, slower execution |

**Sources:** [src/myopts.h:124-125](), [src/myopts.h:140]()

## Common Usage Patterns

### Basic Database Search
```bash
reseek search --db database.bca --input query.fasta --output results.tsv
```

### Sensitive Search with Custom Scoring
```bash
reseek search --db database.bca --input query.fasta --output results.tsv --sensitive --evalue 1e-5 --minscore 50
```

### Format Conversion
```bash
reseek convert --input structures.pdb --output structures.cal --format cal
```

### Benchmarking with ROC Analysis
```bash
reseek scop40bench --db scop40.bca --roc results.roc --benchlevel detailed
```

# Page: Output Formatting

# Output Formatting

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [README.md](README.md)
- [src/usage.h](src/usage.h)
- [src/userfieldnames.h](src/userfieldnames.h)
- [src/userfields.cpp](src/userfields.cpp)

</details>



This document describes the output formatting system in reseek, which provides flexible control over what information is included in search results and how it is presented. The system is built around a configurable field selection mechanism that allows users to specify exactly which columns they want in their output files.

For information about the search commands that generate this output, see [Commands and Options](#6.1). For details about the alignment algorithms that compute these values, see [Core Alignment Engine](#3).

## Overview

The output formatting system is centered around the `USERFIELD` system, which allows users to specify custom output columns via the `-columns` command-line parameter. The system supports both tabular output (via `-output`) and human-readable alignment output (via `-aln`).

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["Command Line"] --> B["-columns param"]
    A --> C["-output param"]
    A --> D["-aln param"]
    
    B --> E["StrToUF()"]
    E --> F["USERFIELD enum"]
    F --> G["DSSAligner::WriteUserField()"]
    
    C --> H["Tabular Output File"]
    D --> I["Alignment Text File"]
    
    G --> H
    G --> I
    
    J["userfieldnames.h"] --> F
    K["Default Fields"] --> F
    L["Standard Fields"] --> F
```

**UserField System Architecture**

Sources: [src/userfields.cpp:1-152](), [src/userfieldnames.h:1-34](), [README.md:36-60]()

## Available Output Fields

The system supports 31 different output fields, each providing specific information about alignments and search results:

| Field Name | Description | Example Value |
|------------|-------------|---------------|
| `query` | Query structure label | `1XYZ_A` |
| `target` | Target structure label | `2ABC_B` |
| `evalue` | E-value from log-linear null model | `1.2e-5` |
| `pvalue` | P-value from log-linear null model | `3.4e-8` |
| `ql` | Query length (residues) | `150` |
| `tl` | Target length (residues) | `200` |
| `qlo` | Alignment start in query (1-based) | `10` |
| `qhi` | Alignment end in query (1-based) | `140` |
| `tlo` | Alignment start in target (1-based) | `15` |
| `thi` | Alignment end in target (1-based) | `180` |
| `pctid` | Percent identity of alignment | `25.3` |
| `cigar` | CIGAR string describing alignment | `20M5D30M` |
| `aq` | Alignment quality (0-1, >0.5 suggests homology) | `0.75` |
| `qrow` | Aligned query sequence with gaps (local) | `ACGT-TTGC` |
| `trow` | Aligned target sequence with gaps (local) | `ACGTATTGC` |
| `qrowg` | Aligned query sequence with gaps (global) | `ACGT-TTGC` |
| `trowg` | Aligned target sequence with gaps (global) | `ACGTATTGC` |

### Statistical and Scoring Fields

| Field Name | Description |
|------------|-------------|
| `ts` | Test statistic |
| `newts` | New test statistic |
| `dpscore` | Dynamic programming score |
| `lddt` | LDDT score |
| `gscore` | Global score |
| `raw` | Raw alignment score |
| `ids` | Number of identities |
| `gaps` | Number of gaps |
| `muhsp` | Mu HSP score |
| `muchain` | Mu chain score |

### Predefined Field Sets

The system provides convenient predefined field combinations:

- **`std`**: Standard fields = `query+target+qlo+qhi+ql+tlo+thi+tl+pctid+evalue`
- **Default**: `aq+query+target+evalue+pvalue` (used when no `-columns` specified)

Sources: [src/userfieldnames.h:1-34](), [README.md:41-59](), [src/usage.h:29-48]()

## Command-Line Usage

### Basic Output Control

```bash
# Use default columns
reseek -search query.pdb -db database.bca -output results.txt

# Specify custom columns
reseek -search query.pdb -db database.bca -output results.txt \
       -columns query+target+evalue+pctid+aq

# Use standard column set
reseek -search query.pdb -db database.bca -output results.txt \
       -columns std

# Generate both tabular and alignment output
reseek -search query.pdb -db database.bca \
       -output results.txt -aln alignments.txt
```

### Output File Types

```mermaid
graph LR
    A["reseek -search"] --> B["-output FILE"]
    A --> C["-aln FILE"]
    
    B --> D["Tabular Results"]
    C --> E["Human-Readable Alignments"]
    
    D --> F["TSV Format"]
    D --> G["Custom Columns"]
    
    E --> H["Sequence Alignments"]
    E --> I["Structure Superposition"]
    
    F --> J["query<tab>target<tab>evalue..."]
    H --> K["Query: ACGT-TTGC<br/>Target: ACGTATTGC"]
```

**Output File Generation Flow**

Sources: [README.md:25-39](), [src/usage.h:25-27]()

## Implementation Architecture

The output formatting system is implemented through several key components:

### Core Components

```mermaid
graph TB
    A["USERFIELD enum"] --> B["StrToUF()"]
    A --> C["UFToStr()"]
    A --> D["DSSAligner::WriteUserField()"]
    
    E["userfieldnames.h"] --> A
    F["userfields.cpp"] --> B
    F --> C
    F --> D
    
    G["Command Line Parser"] --> H["-columns parsing"]
    H --> I["Field Name Strings"]
    I --> B
    
    B --> J["USERFIELD Values"]
    J --> D
    
    D --> K["fprintf() calls"]
    K --> L["Output Files"]
    
    M["DSSAligner State"] --> D
    N["Alignment Results"] --> D
    O["Statistical Values"] --> D
```

**UserField System Implementation**

### Field Name Resolution

The system uses a macro-based approach to define field names and their corresponding enum values:

```cpp
// From userfieldnames.h - defines both enum and string conversion
#define x(name) UF_##name,
enum USERFIELD { 
    #include "userfieldnames.h"
};

// String to enum conversion
USERFIELD StrToUF(const string &Str) {
    #define x(name) if (Str == #name) return UF_##name;
    #include "userfieldnames.h"
    // ... error handling
}
```

### Output Generation

The `WriteUserField` method in `DSSAligner` handles the actual output formatting:

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["WriteUserField(FILE* f, USERFIELD UF, bool Up)"] --> B{"Switch on UF"}
    
    B --> C["UF_query → GetLabel()"]
    B --> D["UF_evalue → GetEvalue()"]
    B --> E["UF_pctid → GetPctId()"]
    B --> F["UF_cigar → PathToCIGAR()"]
    B --> G["UF_qrow → GetRow()"]
    B --> H["Other fields..."]
    
    C --> I["fprintf() output"]
    D --> J["EvalueToStr() formatting"]
    E --> K["%.1f formatting"]
    F --> L["CIGAR string generation"]
    G --> M["Sequence row generation"]
    
    J --> I
    K --> I
    L --> I
    M --> I
    
    I --> N["Output File"]
```

**Field Output Generation Process**

Sources: [src/userfields.cpp:45-151](), [src/userfieldnames.h:1-34]()

## Output Format Examples

### Default Output Format

When no `-columns` parameter is specified, the system outputs:
```
aq      query   target  evalue  pvalue
0.7500  1XYZ_A  2ABC_B  1.2e-5  3.4e-8
0.6200  1XYZ_A  3DEF_C  2.1e-4  5.7e-7
```

### Custom Column Selection

Using `-columns query+target+pctid+cigar+aq`:
```
query   target  pctid   cigar           aq
1XYZ_A  2ABC_B  25.3    20M5D30M2I15M   0.7500
1XYZ_A  3DEF_C  18.7    15M3D25M        0.6200
```

### Standard Format

Using `-columns std`:
```
query   target  qlo qhi ql  tlo thi tl  pctid   evalue
1XYZ_A  2ABC_B  10  140 150 15  180 200 25.3    1.2e-5
1XYZ_A  3DEF_C  5   135 150 20  170 190 18.7    2.1e-4
```

### Alignment Output

The `-aln` parameter generates human-readable alignment files:
```
Query: 1XYZ_A (150 residues)
Target: 2ABC_B (200 residues)
E-value: 1.2e-5, P-value: 3.4e-8, AQ: 0.75

Query   10  ACGTTTGCAAAAATTTGCCC-AAATTTGGGCCCAAATTT  48
            ||||  ||     ||||||| ||| ||||||||||||||
Target  15  ACGTAAGC-----TTTGCCCAAAATTTGGGCCCAAATTT  48
```

Sources: [README.md:36-60](), [src/usage.h:25-48]()

## Special Field Handling

### E-value Formatting

The `EvalueToStr` function provides intelligent formatting for E-values:

- Values > 100: displayed as "100"
- Values > 1: displayed with 1 decimal place (e.g., "2.5")
- Values > 0.001: displayed with 4 decimal places (e.g., "0.0125")
- Values ≤ 0.001: displayed in scientific notation (e.g., "1.25e-4")

### Orientation Handling

The system handles query/target orientation through the `Up` parameter in `WriteUserField`, which determines whether the alignment should be interpreted as Query=A/Target=B or Query=B/Target=A based on the search direction.

### Row Generation

The `qrow`, `trow`, `qrowg`, and `trowg` fields generate aligned sequences with gaps:
- Local alignment rows (`qrow`/`trow`): Show only the aligned portion
- Global alignment rows (`qrowg`/`trowg`): Show the complete alignment including flanking regions

Sources: [src/userfields.cpp:19-30](), [src/userfields.cpp:45-151]()

# Analysis and Benchmarking

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

This section covers the performance evaluation tools, statistical calibration systems, and specialized scoring methods used to assess and optimize the protein structure search capabilities of reseek. The analysis framework provides comprehensive benchmarking against gold standard datasets, statistical model calibration, and multiple scoring methodologies for alignment quality assessment.

For information about the core alignment algorithms being benchmarked, see [Core Alignment Engine](#3). For database search optimization, see [Database Search System](#4).

## SCOP40 Benchmarking Framework

The primary benchmarking system is built around the SCOP40 database, which provides a gold standard for protein structure classification. The `SCOP40Bench` class serves as the foundation for all performance evaluation.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "SCOP40Bench Framework"
        SB[SCOP40Bench]
        DBS[DBSearcher]
        DSS[DSSAligner]
    end
    
    subgraph "Data Management"
        DOM["m_Doms<br/>Domain Labels"]
        SF["m_SFs<br/>Superfamily Classifications"] 
        FOLD["m_Folds<br/>Fold Classifications"]
        CHAIN["m_DBChains<br/>PDB Structures"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Hit Storage"
        SCORES["m_Scores<br/>E-values/Scores"]
        IDX1["m_DomIdx1s<br/>Query Domain Indices"]
        IDX2["m_DomIdx2s<br/>Target Domain Indices"]
        TFS["m_TFs<br/>True/False Classifications"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Analysis Outputs"
        ROC["ROC Curves"]
        SENS["Sensitivity Metrics"]
        SPEC["Specificity Metrics"] 
        EVAL["E-value Statistics"]
    end
    
    SB --> DBS
    SB --> DSS
    SB --> DOM
    SB --> SF
    SB --> FOLD
    SB --> CHAIN
    
    DSS --> SCORES
    DSS --> IDX1
    DSS --> IDX2
    
    SB --> TFS
    SB --> ROC
    SB --> SENS
    SB --> SPEC
    SB --> EVAL
```

**SCOP40Bench Architecture Overview**

The benchmarking system processes protein domain classifications and generates comprehensive performance statistics through ROC analysis and sensitivity measurements.

Sources: [src/scop40bench.h:9-178](), [src/scop40bench.cpp:19-90]()

### Domain Classification and Indexing

The system organizes protein domains according to SCOP hierarchy levels:

| Level | Description | Code Reference |
|-------|-------------|----------------|
| **Superfamily** | `m_Level = "sf"` | Proteins with similar structure and function |
| **Fold** | `m_Level = "fold"` | Proteins with similar overall topology |
| **Family** | Individual protein families | Highest resolution classification |

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "SCOP Label Parsing"
        LABEL["d1a0o.1/a.1.1.1"]
        PARSE[ParseScopLabel]
        DOM["Dom: d1a0o.1"]
        CLS["Class: a"]
        FOLD["Fold: a.1"] 
        SF["Superfamily: a.1.1"]
        FAM["Family: a.1.1.1"]
    end
    
    LABEL --> PARSE
    PARSE --> DOM
    PARSE --> CLS
    PARSE --> FOLD
    PARSE --> SF
    PARSE --> FAM
```

**SCOP Label Processing Pipeline**

The `ParseScopLabel` method extracts hierarchical classification information from domain identifiers for true positive/false positive determination.

Sources: [src/scop40bench.cpp:57-90](), [src/scop40bench.cpp:146-188]()

### True Positive/False Positive Classification

The core evaluation logic determines whether domain pairs represent true positives based on SCOP classification:

```cpp
// Return 1=TP, 0=FP, -1=ignore
int SCOP40Bench::IsT(uint DomIdx1, uint DomIdx2) const
{
    if (m_Level == "sf") {
        if (SFIdx1 == SFIdx2) return 1;  // Same superfamily = TP
        else return 0;                   // Different superfamily = FP
    }
    // Additional logic for fold and family levels
}
```

Sources: [src/scop40benchroc.cpp:166-216]()

## ROC Analysis and Performance Metrics

The system generates Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves to evaluate search sensitivity and specificity across different score thresholds.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "ROC Analysis Pipeline"
        HITS["Hit Collection<br/>m_Scores, m_DomIdx1s, m_DomIdx2s"]
        ORDER["SetScoreOrder()"]
        STEPS["GetROCSteps()"]
        SMOOTH["SmoothROCSteps()"]
        CURVE["GetCurve()"]
    end
    
    subgraph "ROC Metrics"
        TPR["True Positive Rate<br/>Sensitivity"]
        FPR["False Positive Rate<br/>1 - Specificity"]
        EPQ["Errors Per Query"]
        AUC["Area Under Curve"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Output Formats"
        TSV["ROC TSV Files"]
        CVE["CVE Format"]
        SUMMARY["Performance Summary"]
    end
    
    HITS --> ORDER
    ORDER --> STEPS
    STEPS --> SMOOTH
    SMOOTH --> CURVE
    
    STEPS --> TPR
    STEPS --> FPR
    STEPS --> EPQ
    CURVE --> AUC
    
    TPR --> TSV
    FPR --> CVE
    EPQ --> SUMMARY
    AUC --> SUMMARY
```

**ROC Analysis Workflow**

The ROC analysis processes alignment hits through multiple stages to generate comprehensive performance statistics and visualization data.

Sources: [src/scop40benchroc.cpp:454-513](), [src/scop40benchroc.cpp:325-391]()

### Key Performance Metrics

The benchmarking system calculates several critical performance indicators:

| Metric | Formula | Description |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| **TPR (Sensitivity)** | `TP / (TP + FN)` | Fraction of true relationships detected |
| **FPR** | `FP / (FP + TN)` | Fraction of false alarms |
| **EPQ** | `FP / QueryCount` | Expected false positives per query |
| **Sens@1FP** | Special calculation | Sensitivity before first false positive |

Sources: [src/scop40bench.cpp:523-541](), [src/scop40bench.cpp:587-611]()

## Statistical Calibration

The calibration subsystem fits statistical models to test statistic distributions for accurate E-value calculation.

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "CalibrateSearcher System"
        CS[CalibrateSearcher]
        SB40[SCOP40Bench]
        TSV["m_TestStatsVec<br/>Per-Chain Statistics"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Distribution Fitting"
        BINS["Binner<br/>Histogram Generation"]
        GUMBEL["Gumbel Distribution<br/>m_GumbelMu, m_GumbelBeta"]
        NORMAL["Normal Distribution<br/>m_NormalMean, m_NormalSigma"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Calibration Methods"
        CAL1[calibrate<br/>All-domain]
        CAL2[calibrate2<br/>Linear Fit]
        CAL3[calibrate3<br/>Per-chain TS Bins]
    end
    
    CS --> SB40
    CS --> TSV
    TSV --> BINS
    BINS --> GUMBEL
    BINS --> NORMAL
    
    CS --> CAL1
    CS --> CAL2
    CS --> CAL3
```

**Statistical Calibration Architecture**

The calibration system extends SCOP40Bench to collect test statistics and fit probability distributions for E-value computation.

Sources: [src/calibratesearcher.h:12-58](), [src/calibrate.cpp:12-45]()

### Distribution Fitting Methods

The system supports multiple approaches to statistical calibration:

**Gumbel Distribution Fitting:**
- Used for extreme value statistics of alignment scores
- Implemented in `FitGumbel()` method
- Parameters: `m_GumbelMu` (location), `m_GumbelBeta` (scale)

**Per-Chain Calibration:**
- Collects test statistics for each database chain
- Bins statistics into histograms for distribution analysis
- Accounts for sequence length and composition effects

Sources: [src/calibratesearcher.cpp:132-142](), [src/calibrate3.cpp:242-360]()

## Specialized Scoring Methods

### DALI Scoring Implementation

The DALI (Distance matrix ALIgnment) scoring system provides an alternative structural similarity metric based on distance matrices.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph "DALIScorer Framework"
        DS[DALIScorer]
        MSA["Multiple Sequence Alignment"]
        CHAINS["PDB Chain Structures"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Distance Analysis"
        DISTMX["m_DistMxVec<br/>Distance Matrices"]
        CORE["m_ColIsCore<br/>Core Column Detection"]
        COLPOS["m_ColToPosVec<br/>Column to Position Mapping"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Scoring Components"
        OFFDIAG["Off-diagonal Score<br/>Distance Comparison"]
        DIAG["Diagonal Score<br/>Alignment Length * Theta"]
        ZSCORE["Z-score Calculation"]
    end
    
    DS --> MSA
    DS --> CHAINS
    DS --> DISTMX
    DS --> CORE
    DS --> COLPOS
    
    DISTMX --> OFFDIAG
    CORE --> DIAG
    COLPOS --> ZSCORE
    
    OFFDIAG --> ZSCORE
    DIAG --> ZSCORE
```

**DALI Scoring System Architecture**

The DALI scorer processes multiple sequence alignments and structure data to compute distance-based similarity scores with statistical significance.

Sources: [src/daliscorer.h:10-99](), [src/daliscorer.cpp:75-98]()

### DALI Score Calculation

The DALI score combines distance matrix comparisons with alignment length penalties:

```cpp
double DALIScore = OffDiagScore + Lali * g_DALI_Theta;
double Z = GetDALIZFromScoreAndLengths(DALIScore, QL, TL);
```

**Key Parameters:**
- `g_DALI_D = 20.0` - Envelope radius for distance weighting
- `g_DALI_d0 = 0.2` - Distance tolerance parameter  
- `g_DALI_Theta = 0.2` - Diagonal score contribution per aligned position

Sources: [src/dali.cpp:93-110](), [src/daliscorer.cpp:187-226]()

## Command-Line Interface for Analysis

The analysis and benchmarking tools are accessible through several specialized commands:

| Command | Purpose | Key Options |
|---------|---------|-------------|
| `scop40bench` | Full SCOP40 benchmarking | `-benchlevel`, `-maxfpr`, `-roc` |
| `calibrate` | Statistical calibration | `-sensitive`, `-output` |
| `calibrate2` | Linear fit calibration | `-benchlevel`, `-maxfpr` |
| `calibrate3` | Per-chain TS binning | `-calib_output`, `-calib_output2` |
| `daliscore_msa` | DALI scoring for MSA | `-input`, `-core` |

### Example Benchmarking Workflow

```bash
# Run SCOP40 benchmark with ROC analysis
reseek -scop40bench scop40_family.cal -roc results.tsv -curve curve.tsv

# Perform statistical calibration  
reseek -calibrate scop40_family.cal -output calibration.tsv

# Generate DALI scores for MSA
reseek -daliscore_msa alignment.fasta -input structures.cal -output dali_scores.tsv
```

Sources: [src/scop40bench.cpp:767-824](), [src/calibrate.cpp:12-45](), [src/daliscore_msa.cpp:6-54]()

The analysis and benchmarking framework provides comprehensive tools for evaluating protein structure search performance, from gold standard database comparison to statistical calibration and specialized scoring methodologies. This enables systematic optimization and validation of the core alignment algorithms.

# Page: SCOP40 Benchmarking

# SCOP40 Benchmarking

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

This document covers the SCOP40 benchmarking system used for evaluating protein structure search performance in reseek. The system performs ROC analysis against the SCOP40 gold standard database to measure search sensitivity and specificity.

For information about the core alignment engine being benchmarked, see [Core Alignment Engine](#3). For database search implementation details, see [Database Search System](#4).

## System Overview

The SCOP40 benchmarking system evaluates protein structure search algorithms using the Structural Classification of Proteins (SCOP) database as ground truth. It performs comprehensive ROC analysis to generate sensitivity metrics at various error rate thresholds.

### SCOP40Bench Class Architecture

```mermaid

    end
    
    subgraph "ROC Analysis"
        SetTFs["SetTFs()<br/>True/False Assignment"]
        GetROCSteps["GetROCSteps()<br/>ROC Calculation"]
        ROCMetrics["ROC Metrics<br/>SEPQ0.1, SEPQ1, SEPQ10"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Output Generation"
        WriteSummary["WriteSummary()<br/>Results Output"]
        WriteCurve["WriteCurve()<br/>ROC Curve Data"]
        WriteBit["WriteBit()<br/>Binary Results"]
    end
    
    DBSearcher --> SCOP40Bench

```

Sources: [src/scop40bench.h:9-178](), [src/scop40bench.cpp:133-144]()

## SCOP Domain Classification System

The system uses hierarchical protein structure classification to determine true and false positives:

### Domain Label Format and Parsing

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "SCOP Label Structure"
        DomainLabel["d1a0o__ /a.1.1.1<br/>Domain/Class.Fold.SF.Family"]
        DomainPart["d1a0o__<br/>Domain ID"]
        ScopPart["a.1.1.1<br/>SCOP Classification"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Parsed Components"
        Class["a<br/>Class"]
        Fold["a.1<br/>Fold"]
        SF["a.1.1<br/>Superfamily"]
        Family["a.1.1.1<br/>Family"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Index Maps"
        DomToIdx["m_DomToIdx<br/>Domain → Index"]
        SFToIdx["m_SFToIdx<br/>SF → Index"]
        FoldToIdx["m_FoldToIdx<br/>Fold → Index"]
    end
    
    DomainLabel --> DomainPart
    DomainLabel --> ScopPart
    ScopPart --> Class
    ScopPart --> Fold
    ScopPart --> SF
    ScopPart --> Family
    
    Class --> DomToIdx
    Fold --> FoldToIdx
    SF --> SFToIdx
    Family --> SFToIdx
```

The `ParseScopLabel` function extracts hierarchical classification from domain labels:

| Level | Format | Example | Description |
|-------|--------|---------|-------------|
| Class | `a` | `a` | Protein class |
| Fold | `a.1` | `a.1` | Structural fold |
| Superfamily | `a.1.1` | `a.1.1` | Superfamily |
| Family | `a.1.1.1` | `a.1.1.1` | Family |

Sources: [src/scop40bench.cpp:57-90](), [src/scop40bench.cpp:29-40]()

### True/False Positive Determination

```mermaid
graph TD
    PairComparison["Domain Pair Comparison<br/>Dom1, Dom2"]
    
    subgraph "Classification Levels"
        SFLevel["m_Level = 'sf'<br/>Superfamily Level"]
        FoldLevel["m_Level = 'fold'<br/>Fold Level"]
        IgnoreLevel["m_Level = 'ignore'<br/>Ignore Same-fold"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Decision Logic"
        SameIdx["Same Index?"]
        DifferentIdx["Different Index?"]
        TPResult["Return 1 (TP)"]
        FPResult["Return 0 (FP)"]
        IgnoreResult["Return -1 (Ignore)"]
    end
    
    PairComparison --> SFLevel
    PairComparison --> FoldLevel
    PairComparison --> IgnoreLevel
    
    SFLevel --> SameIdx
    FoldLevel --> SameIdx
    IgnoreLevel --> SameIdx
    
    SameIdx -->|Yes| TPResult
    SameIdx -->|No| DifferentIdx
    DifferentIdx -->|Yes| FPResult
    DifferentIdx -->|Special Cases| IgnoreResult
```

The `IsT` function determines classification based on the benchmarking level:

```cpp
int SCOP40Bench::IsT(uint DomIdx1, uint DomIdx2) const
{
    if (m_Level == "sf") {
        if (SFIdx1 == SFIdx2) return 1;  // TP
        else return 0;  // FP
    }
    // Similar logic for fold and ignore levels
}
```

Sources: [src/scop40benchroc.cpp:166-216]()

## ROC Analysis and Metrics

### ROC Calculation Workflow

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Data Preparation"
        StoreScore["StoreScore()<br/>Collect Alignment Scores"]
        SetTFs["SetTFs()<br/>Assign True/False Labels"]
        SetScoreOrder["SetScoreOrder()<br/>Sort by Score"]
    end
    
    subgraph "ROC Step Generation"
        GetROCSteps["GetROCSteps()<br/>Generate ROC Points"]
        CurrentScore["Current Score Threshold"]
        NTP["Count True Positives"]
        NFP["Count False Positives"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Metrics Calculation"
        TPR["TPR = NTP / m_NT<br/>True Positive Rate"]
        EPQ["EPQ = NFP / QueryCount<br/>Errors Per Query"]
        Thresholds["SEPQ Thresholds<br/>0.1, 1.0, 10.0"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Output Generation"
        SmoothROC["SmoothROCSteps()<br/>Smooth Curve"]
        WriteCurve["WriteCurve()<br/>Export Data"]
        WriteSummary["WriteSummary()<br/>Final Metrics"]
    end
    
    StoreScore --> SetTFs
    SetTFs --> SetScoreOrder
    SetScoreOrder --> GetROCSteps
    GetROCSteps --> CurrentScore
    CurrentScore --> NTP
    CurrentScore --> NFP
    NTP --> TPR
    NFP --> EPQ
    TPR --> Thresholds
    EPQ --> Thresholds
    Thresholds --> SmoothROC
    SmoothROC --> WriteCurve
    SmoothROC --> WriteSummary
```

### Key Performance Metrics

The system calculates several standard benchmarking metrics:

| Metric | Description | Calculation |
|--------|-------------|-------------|
| `m_nt_epq0_1` | True positives at EPQ ≤ 0.1 | `GetNTPAtEPQThreshold(0.1)` |
| `m_nt_epq1` | True positives at EPQ ≤ 1.0 | `GetNTPAtEPQThreshold(1.0)` |
| `m_nt_epq10` | True positives at EPQ ≤ 10.0 | `GetNTPAtEPQThreshold(10.0)` |
| `m_nt_firstfp` | Sensitivity to first FP | `GetSens1stFP()` |
| `m_Area` | Area under ROC curve | `GetArea(TPRs, Log10EPQs)` |

Sources: [src/scop40benchroc.cpp:454-513](), [src/scop40bench.cpp:566-585]()

### Command Entry Point

The main benchmarking command is `cmd_scop40bench()` which:

1. Loads the SCOP40 database from `.cal` format
2. Initializes `DSSParams` for alignment configuration
3. Executes all-vs-all search using `RunSelf()`
4. Processes results and generates performance metrics
5. Outputs summary statistics and detailed results

Sources: [src/scop40bench.cpp:767-824]()

### Benchmark Levels

The system supports different classification levels via `m_Level`:

- `"sf"` - Superfamily level (default)
- `"fold"` - Fold level
- `"ignore"` - Ignore same-fold different-superfamily pairs

## Output and Results

### Result Files Generated

| File Type | Function | Description |
|-----------|----------|-------------|
| CVE | `WriteCVE()` | Curve vs E-value data |
| ROC | `ROCStepsToTsv()` | ROC curve points |
| Curve | `WriteCurve()` | Smoothed curve data |
| Summary | `WriteSummary()` | Performance metrics |
| Binary | `WriteBit()` | Compressed results |

### Performance Summary Format

```
SEPQ0.1=0.2107 SEPQ1=0.3144 SEPQ10=0.3882 Area=7.14 secs=120 [git-version]
```

Where:
- `SEPQ0.1` = Sensitivity at 0.1 errors per query
- `SEPQ1` = Sensitivity at 1.0 errors per query  
- `SEPQ10` = Sensitivity at 10.0 errors per query
- `Area` = Area under ROC curve
- `secs` = Execution time

Sources: [src/scop40bench.cpp:587-611](), [src/scop40bench.cpp:660-676]()

# Page: Statistical Calibration

# Statistical Calibration

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [src/calibrate.cpp](src/calibrate.cpp)
- [src/calibrate2.cpp](src/calibrate2.cpp)
- [src/calibrate3.cpp](src/calibrate3.cpp)
- [src/calibrate5.cpp](src/calibrate5.cpp)
- [src/calibratesearcher.cpp](src/calibratesearcher.cpp)
- [src/calibratesearcher.h](src/calibratesearcher.h)

</details>



## Purpose and Scope

The Statistical Calibration system provides methods for calibrating statistical models used in protein structure search scoring. This module fits empirical distributions of test statistics to theoretical distributions (Gumbel and Normal) to enable accurate calculation of E-values and P-values for search results. The calibration is essential for determining the statistical significance of structural alignments and controlling false positive rates in database searches.

For information about the broader benchmarking framework that uses these calibrated statistics, see [SCOP40 Benchmarking](#7.1). For details about the core alignment scoring system that generates the test statistics being calibrated, see [Core Alignment Engine](#3).

## Calibration System Architecture

The calibration system is built around the `CalibrateSearcher` class and provides multiple calibration approaches for different use cases:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Command Interface"
        CMD1["cmd_calibrate()"]
        CMD2["cmd_calibrate2()"]
        CMD3["cmd_calibrate3()"]
        CMD5["cmd_calibrate5()"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Core Calibration"
        CS["CalibrateSearcher"]
        SB["SCOP40Bench"]
        DBS["DBSearcher"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Distribution Fitting"
        GUMBEL["FitGumbel()"]
        NORMAL["FitNormal()"]
        LINEAR["LinearFit()"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Data Processing"
        BINNER["Binner<float>"]
        STATS["Test Statistics"]
        BINS["Binned Data"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Statistical Models"
        EVALUES["E-values"]
        PVALUES["P-values"]
        DIST["Distribution Parameters"]
    end
    
    CMD1 --> CS
    CMD2 --> SB
    CMD3 --> CS
    CMD5 --> DBS
    
    CS --> SB
    SB --> DBS
    
    CS --> GUMBEL
    CS --> NORMAL
    CMD2 --> LINEAR
    
    STATS --> BINNER
    BINNER --> BINS
    BINS --> GUMBEL
    BINS --> NORMAL
    
    GUMBEL --> DIST
    NORMAL --> DIST
    LINEAR --> DIST
    
    DIST --> EVALUES
    DIST --> PVALUES
```

**Sources:** [src/calibratesearcher.h:1-61](), [src/calibrate.cpp:1-46](), [src/calibrate2.cpp:1-143](), [src/calibrate3.cpp:1-361](), [src/calibrate5.cpp:1-110]()

## Core Calibration Workflow

The calibration process follows a systematic workflow for collecting test statistics, binning them, and fitting distributions:

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Data Collection"
        QUERY["Query Structures"]
        DB["Database Structures"]
        ALN["DSSAligner"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Test Statistic Collection"
        ONALN["OnAln()"]
        TSVEC["m_TestStatsVec"]
        HITIDX["m_HitChainIdxs"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Preprocessing"
        SCANALL["ScanAll()"]
        OUTLIERS["Remove Outliers"]
        ALLTS["m_AllTSs"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Binning Process"
        SETBINS["SetAllBins()"]
        BINNER["m_ptrAllBinner"]
        BINS["m_AllBins"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Distribution Fitting"
        SETXY["Setxys()"]
        FITDIST["FitGumbel() / FitNormal()"]
        PARAMS["Distribution Parameters"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Output Generation"
        WRITEBINS["WriteBins()"]
        RESULTS["Calibration Results"]
    end
    
    QUERY --> ALN
    DB --> ALN
    ALN --> ONALN
    ONALN --> TSVEC
    ONALN --> HITIDX
    
    TSVEC --> SCANALL

    OUTLIERS --> ALLTS

    BINNER --> BINS

    FITDIST --> PARAMS

```

**Sources:** [src/calibratesearcher.cpp:32-56](), [src/calibratesearcher.cpp:175-199](), [src/calibratesearcher.cpp:104-130](), [src/calibratesearcher.cpp:71-102]()

## Calibration Approaches

The system provides four distinct calibration approaches, each suited for different scenarios:

### Standard Calibration (`cmd_calibrate`)

The standard calibration approach performs all-vs-all comparison within a database and fits a Gumbel distribution to false positive scores:

| Feature | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| **Input** | Single database file (used as both query and database) |
| **Method** | Gumbel distribution fitting |
| **Output** | Binned distribution with fitted parameters |
| **Use Case** | General-purpose calibration for E-value calculation |

### Linear Calibration (`cmd_calibrate2`)

This approach uses linear regression to fit test statistics to negative log P-values:

| Feature | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| **Input** | SCOP40 database |
| **Method** | Linear fit: `y = mx + b` where `y = -log(P)` |
| **Parameters** | Superfamily: m=20.5, b=2.89; Fold: m=26.6, b=2.42 |
| **Range** | NFP between NQ/100 and NQ*100 |

### Per-Chain Calibration (`cmd_calibrate3`)

The most sophisticated approach that generates training data for machine learning models:

| Feature | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| **Bins** | 16 bins for test statistics (0.0 to 1.0) |
| **Features** | Per-chain test statistic histograms |
| **Sampling** | Balanced TP/FP sampling with noise injection |
| **Output** | Training data with features and labels |

### Query-Specific Calibration (`cmd_calibrate5`)

Collects test statistics and dynamic programming scores for each query structure:

| Feature | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| **Mode** | Very sensitive search mode |
| **Tracking** | Both test statistics and DP scores |
| **Output** | Per-query score distributions |

**Sources:** [src/calibrate.cpp:12-45](), [src/calibrate2.cpp:54-142](), [src/calibrate3.cpp:242-360](), [src/calibrate5.cpp:89-109]()

## Distribution Fitting Methods

The calibration system supports two primary distribution types for modeling test statistics:

### Gumbel Distribution

The Gumbel distribution is the primary model for fitting false positive score distributions:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Gumbel Fitting Process"
        PARAMS["Distribution Parameters"]
        MU["m_GumbelMu"]
        BETA["m_GumbelBeta"]
        SCALE["m_GumbelScale"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Input Data"
        XY["m_ys (normalized frequencies)"]
        X0["m_x0 (starting x value)"]
        DX["m_dx (bin width)"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Fitting Function"
        FITGUMBEL["fit_gumbel()"]
        EXTERNAL["External fitting routine"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Statistical Functions"
        PDF["gumbel() - PDF"]
        CDF["gumbel_cdf() - CDF"]
        EVALUE["E-value calculation"]
    end
    
    XY --> FITGUMBEL
    X0 --> FITGUMBEL
    DX --> FITGUMBEL
    
    FITGUMBEL --> EXTERNAL
    EXTERNAL --> PARAMS
    
    PARAMS --> MU
    PARAMS --> BETA
    PARAMS --> SCALE
    
    MU --> PDF
    BETA --> PDF
    PDF --> CDF
    CDF --> EVALUE
```

### Normal Distribution

The Normal distribution provides an alternative model for certain calibration scenarios:

| Parameter | Description | Calculation |
|-----------|-------------|-------------|
| **Mean** | `m_NormalMean` | Weighted average: `Σ(x*y) / Σ(y)` |
| **Sigma** | `m_NormalSigma` | Standard deviation: `√(Σ(y*(x-μ)²))` |

**Sources:** [src/calibratesearcher.cpp:132-142](), [src/calibratesearcher.cpp:144-173](), [src/calibratesearcher.cpp:8-16]()

## Binning and Data Processing

The calibration system uses sophisticated binning strategies to handle test statistic distributions:

### Binning Configuration

| Parameter | Value | Purpose |
|-----------|-------|---------|
| **NBINS** | 101 | Number of bins for distribution fitting |
| **NOUTLIERS** | 3 | Number of outliers to discard per chain |
| **BIN_COUNT** | 16 | Bins for per-chain calibration |

### Data Transformation

Test statistics undergo logarithmic transformation for better distribution fitting:

```cpp
// Transform: TS -> -log(TS)
float logTs = -logf(TS);
```

### Outlier Handling

The system automatically removes outliers to improve distribution fitting:

- Discards top 3 scores per chain (`NOUTLIERS = 3`)
- Trims low-frequency bins near x=0 during curve fitting
- Normalizes bin frequencies to create proper probability distributions

**Sources:** [src/calibratesearcher.cpp:104-130](), [src/calibratesearcher.cpp:175-199](), [src/calibratesearcher.h:59-61]()

## Command-Line Interface

Each calibration command provides specific options and outputs:

### Common Parameters

| Parameter | Description | Default |
|-----------|-------------|---------|
| `--sensitive` | Use sensitive search mode | Automatically set |
| `--minchainlength` | Minimum chain length | 1 |
| `--evalue` | E-value threshold | 10 |

### Output Options

| Option | Purpose | Format |
|--------|---------|---------|
| `--calib_output` | Main calibration output | Binned distributions |
| `--calib_output2` | TP/FP bin counts | Per-domain statistics |
| `--calib_output3` | ML training data | Feature vectors with labels |
| `--calib_output5a` | Test statistics per query | Tab-separated values |
| `--calib_output5b` | DP scores per query | Tab-separated values |

### Usage Examples

```bash
# Standard calibration
reseek -calibrate database.cal -calib_output results.tsv

# Linear calibration with SCOP40
reseek -calibrate2 scop40.cal -benchlevel sf -output linear_fit.tsv

# Per-chain calibration for ML training
reseek -calibrate3 database.cal -calib_output bins.tsv -calib_output2 tpfp.tsv -calib_output3 features.tsv

# Query-specific calibration
reseek -calibrate5 query.fasta -db database.cal -calib_output5a ts_scores.tsv -calib_output5b dp_scores.tsv
```

**Sources:** [src/calibrate.cpp:12-45](), [src/calibrate2.cpp:54-142](), [src/calibrate3.cpp:242-360](), [src/calibrate5.cpp:89-109]()

# Page: Specialized Scoring Methods

# Specialized Scoring Methods

<details>
<summary>Relevant source files</summary>

The following files were used as context for generating this wiki page:

- [src/dali.cpp](src/dali.cpp)
- [src/daliscore_msa.cpp](src/daliscore_msa.cpp)
- [src/daliscore_tsv.cpp](src/daliscore_tsv.cpp)

- [src/daliscorer.h](src/daliscorer.h)

</details>



This page documents the specialized scoring algorithms implemented in reseek for evaluating protein structure alignments and multiple sequence alignments. These methods complement the core alignment engine by providing standardized metrics for structural similarity assessment.

For general alignment scoring and configuration, see [Parameter Configuration](#3.2). For benchmarking and performance evaluation workflows, see [SCOP40 Benchmarking](#7.1) and [Statistical Calibration](#7.2).

## DALI Scoring System

The DALI (Distance Alignment) scoring system is the primary specialized scoring method implemented in reseek. It evaluates structural similarity by comparing intramolecular distance matrices between aligned protein structures.

### Core Algorithm

The DALI scoring algorithm is implemented through the `DALI_dpscorefun` function, which computes similarity scores based on distance differences between corresponding residue pairs:

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["`DALI_dpscorefun(a, b)`"] --> B["`diff = |a - b|`"]
    A --> C["`mean = (a + b) / 2`"]
    B --> D["`ratio = diff / mean`"]
    C --> E["`weight = Weight(mean)`"]
    D --> F["`score = weight * (d0 - ratio)`"]
    E --> F
    F --> G["`Final DALI Score`"]
    
    H["`Weight Function`"] --> I["`exp(-x * y²) lookup table`"]
    I --> E
```

The algorithm uses configurable parameters:
- `g_DALI_D = 20.0` - envelope radius for weight calculation
- `g_DALI_d0 = 0.2` - base distance threshold  
- `g_DALI_Theta = 0.2` - diagonal contribution weight

Sources: [src/dali.cpp:93-110](), [src/dali.cpp:23-40]()

### DALIScorer Class Architecture

The `DALIScorer` class provides the primary interface for DALI scoring operations:

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class DALIScorer {
        +string m_Name
        +const SeqDB* m_MSA
        +vector~PDBChain*~ m_Chains
        +map~string,uint~ m_SeqToChainIdx
        +vector~uint~ m_SeqIdxToChainIdx
        +vector~vector~double~~ m_DistMxVec
        +LoadChains(string FN)
        +SetMSA(string Name, SeqDB MSA, bool DoCore, bool MissingSeqOk)
        +GetDALIScore_ChainPair(uint ChainIdx1, uint ChainIdx2, vector~uint~ Pos1s, vector~uint~ Pos2s)
        +GetZ() double
        +GetDALIRowPair(uint SeqIdx1, uint SeqIdx2, double Score, double Z)
    }
    
    class PDBChain {
        +string m_Label
        +string m_Seq
        +GetDist(uint Pos1, uint Pos2) double
        +GetSeqLength() uint
    }
    
    class SeqDB {
        +GetSeqCount() uint
        +GetColCount() uint
        +GetSeq(uint SeqIdx) string
    }
    
    DALIScorer --> PDBChain : loads multiple chains
    DALIScorer --> SeqDB : processes MSA
```

Sources: [src/daliscorer.h:10-99](), [src/daliscorer.cpp:75-98]()

### MSA Processing Workflow

The DALI scoring system processes multiple sequence alignments through a structured workflow:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["`cmd_daliscore_msa()`"] --> B["`SeqDB.FromFasta()`"]
    B --> C["`DALIScorer.LoadChains()`"]
    C --> D["`DALIScorer.SetMSA()`"]
    D --> E["`SetSeqIdxToChainIdx()`"]
    E --> F["`SetCore()` if core mode"]
    F --> G["`SetColToPosVec()`"]
    G --> H["`SetDistMxs()`"]
    H --> I["`Calculate pairwise scores`"]
    I --> J["`GetDALIRowPair()` for each pair"]
    J --> K["`Output results`"]
    
    L["`GetAlignedPositions()`"] --> M["`Extract aligned residue positions`"]
    M --> N["`GetDALIScore_ChainPair()`"]
    N --> O["`GetDALIZFromScoreAndLengths()`"]
    
    J --> L
    O --> K
```

The workflow supports both full alignment and core-only modes, where core positions are defined as columns with minimal gaps and consistent case.

Sources: [src/daliscore_msa.cpp:6-54](), [src/daliscorer.cpp:164-185]()

## LDDT Scoring Methods

Local Distance Difference Test (LDDT) provides an alternative structural similarity metric focusing on local distance preservation within defined radius thresholds.

### LDDT Configuration

The `DALIScorer` class includes LDDT-specific parameters:

| Parameter | Default Value | Purpose |
|-----------|---------------|---------|
| `m_LDDT_R0` | 15.0 | Reference radius for local environment |
| `m_LDDT_thresholds` | [0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0] | Distance difference thresholds |
| `m_LDDT_symm` | `SYMM_First` | Symmetry handling mode |

### LDDT Implementation Methods

The class provides multiple LDDT calculation approaches:

```mermaid
graph LR
    A["`LDDT Methods`"] --> B["`GetLDDT_foldmason()`"]
    A --> C["`GetLDDT_muscle()`"]
    A --> D["`GetLDDTColScore_foldmason()`"]
    A --> E["`GetLDDTChainPair_muscle()`"]
    A --> F["`GetLDDTMuWCol()`"]
    A --> G["`GetLDDTMuW1()`"]
    
    B --> H["`Column-based scoring`"]
    C --> I["`Pairwise chain scoring`"]
    D --> J["`Single column analysis`"]
    E --> K["`Chain pair analysis`"]
    F --> L["`Windowed column scoring`"]
    G --> M["`Single residue window`"]
```

Sources: [src/daliscorer.h:87-98]()

## Implementation Architecture

### Distance Matrix Management

The scoring system maintains precomputed distance matrices for efficient score calculation:

```mermaid
graph TD
    A["`SetDistMxs()`"] --> B["`m_DistMxVec.resize(ChainCount)`"]
    B --> C["`For each chain in MSA`"]
    C --> D["`SetDistMx(ChainIdx)`"]
    D --> E["`Chain.GetDist(i, j)`"]
    E --> F["`DistMx[i][j] = distance`"]
    F --> G["`Symmetric matrix storage`"]
    
    H["`GetDist(ChainId, Pos1, Pos2)`"] --> I["`m_DistMxVec[ChainId][Pos1][Pos2]`"]
    I --> J["`O(1) distance lookup`"]
```

This approach trades memory for computation speed by precomputing all pairwise distances within each protein chain.

Sources: [src/daliscorer.cpp:518-534](), [src/daliscorer.cpp:481-491]()

### Core Position Detection

The system implements core position detection for focused scoring on well-aligned regions:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["`SetCore()`"] --> B["`For each column in MSA`"]
    B --> C["`Count gaps: MSA.GetGapCount(Col)`"]
    C --> D["`Count uppercase: MSA.GetUpperCount(Col)`"]
    D --> E["`Count lowercase: MSA.GetLowerCount(Col)`"]
    E --> F["`MaxGaps = SeqCount/10 + 1`"]
    F --> G{"`gaps ≤ MaxGaps AND lowercase = 0`"}
    G -->|Yes| H["`m_ColIsCore[Col] = true`"]
    G -->|No| I["`m_ColIsCore[Col] = false`"]
    H --> J["`m_CoreColCount++`"]
    I --> J
    J --> K["`Next column`"]
```

Sources: [src/daliscorer.cpp:112-132]()

## Command-Line Interface

### daliscore_msa Command

The `cmd_daliscore_msa` command provides MSA-based DALI scoring:

```bash
reseek -daliscore_msa input.fasta -input chains.pdb -output results.tsv
```

Key options:
- `-core` - Use core positions only
- `-missingtestseqok` - Allow missing sequences in chain database

Output format includes pairwise scores and Z-values for all sequence pairs in the MSA.

### daliscore_tsv Command

The `cmd_daliscore_tsv` command processes existing TSV alignment files:

```bash
reseek -daliscore_tsv alignment.tsv -input chains.pdb -output validated.tsv
```

This command validates and recalculates DALI scores from alignment data, useful for benchmarking and validation workflows.

Sources: [src/daliscore_msa.cpp:6-54](), [src/daliscore_tsv.cpp:28-93]()

### Statistical Output

Both commands generate statistical summaries including:
- Individual pairwise DALI scores
- Z-scores based on sequence length normalization
- Average Z-score across all pairs
- Core vs. full alignment comparisons

The Z-score calculation uses the formula: `Z = (Score - mean) / sigma` where mean and sigma are functions of sequence lengths as implemented in `GetDALIZFromScoreAndLengths`.

Sources: [src/daliscorer.cpp:19-29](), [src/daliscorer.cpp:228-281]()

This document covers the internal developer infrastructure supporting the reseek protein search tool, including core utilities, memory management, build system integration, and fundamental data structures. This material is essential for understanding the codebase architecture and for contributing to the project.

For information about the core alignment algorithms, see [Core Alignment Engine](#3). For database search implementation details, see [Database Search System](#4). For build and deployment processes, see [Build System and CI/CD](#8.1).

## Core Application Architecture

The reseek application follows a command-dispatch architecture where the main entry point processes command-line arguments and dispatches to appropriate command implementations.

### Application Entry Point

The application entry point in `reseek_main.cpp` implements a structured initialization and command dispatch system:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Application Startup"
        main["main()"] --> cmdline["MyCmdLine()"]
        cmdline --> logging["LogProgramInfoAndCmdLine()"]
        logging --> timing["InitTiming()"]
        timing --> memsetup["Memory Setup"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Command Processing"
        memsetup --> cmdcount["Command Count Validation"]
        cmdcount --> dispatch["Command Dispatch"]
        dispatch --> cmd_convert["cmd_convert()"]
        dispatch --> cmd_search["cmd_search()"]
        dispatch --> cmd_bench["cmd_bench()"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Application Cleanup"
        cmd_convert --> cleanup["Cleanup Phase"]
        cmd_search --> cleanup
        cmd_bench --> cleanup
        cleanup --> logtiming["LogTiming()"]
        logtiming --> logmem["LogElapsedTimeAndRAM()"]
        logmem --> exit["MyutilsExit()"]
    end
```

**Application Entry Point Flow**

The main function [src/reseek_main.cpp:10-65]() follows a strict initialization sequence:

1. **Command-line Processing**: `MyCmdLine()` parses arguments and sets global option variables
2. **Logging Initialization**: `LogProgramInfoAndCmdLine()` sets up logging and records program start
3. **Memory Tracking**: Optional memory allocation tracking based on command-line flags
4. **Command Validation**: Ensures exactly one command is specified using preprocessor macros
5. **Command Dispatch**: Uses preprocessor expansion to call the appropriate `cmd_*()` function
6. **Cleanup**: Logs timing, memory usage, and performs orderly shutdown

Sources: [src/reseek_main.cpp:10-65]()

## Core Utility System

**Platform-Specific Implementations**

The utility system provides platform-specific implementations for:

- **Memory Usage Tracking**: Windows (`GetProcessMemoryInfo`), Linux (`/proc/*/statm`), macOS (`task_info`)
- **File I/O**: 64-bit file operations with platform-specific seeks and tells
- **Physical Memory Detection**: Platform-specific methods for determining available RAM
- **Directory Listing**: Windows (`FindFirstFile`/`FindNextFile`) vs Unix (`opendir`/`readdir`)

Sources: [src/myutils.cpp:77-104](), [src/myutils.cpp:832-960](), [src/myutils.cpp:962-1012]()

### I/O Abstraction Layer

The I/O system provides a comprehensive wrapper around standard C file operations with enhanced error handling and 64-bit support:

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "File Management"
        OpenStdioFile["OpenStdioFile()"] --> bufalloc["AllocBuffer()"]

    end
```

**I/O Features**

Key I/O system capabilities include:

- **Buffered I/O**: Custom buffer allocation with `MY_IO_BUFSIZ` (32KB) for performance
- **64-bit File Support**: Full 64-bit file positioning and size operations
- **Error Handling**: Comprehensive error reporting with file state logging
- **File Tracking**: Global map tracking file handles to filenames for debugging
- **Memory Mapped Reading**: Large file reading with chunked operations

Sources: [src/myutils.cpp:158-183](), [src/myutils.cpp:248-287](), [src/myutils.cpp:416-462]()

## Memory Management System

The reseek application implements a sophisticated memory management system with optional debugging capabilities, performance tracking, and leak detection.

### Memory Management Architecture

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Memory Interface"
        myalloc["myalloc(type, count)"] --> mymalloc["mymalloc()"]
        myfree["myfree(ptr)"] --> actualfree["free()"]
        newop["operator new"] --> mymalloc
        deleteop["operator delete"] --> myfree
    end
    
    subgraph "Debug Mode (MYMALLOC_DBG)"
        mymalloc --> memdata["mem_data block"]
        memdata --> magic["magic number"]
        memdata --> tracking["allocation tracking"]
        memdata --> metadata["filename:line info"]
        tracking --> blocklist["s_BlockList"]
        blocklist --> summary["periodic summaries"]
        summary --> statedump["state dumping"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Release Mode"
        mymalloc --> stdlib["standard malloc()"]
        stdlib --> performance["optimized performance"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Statistics"
        g_myalloc_netbytes["g_myalloc_netbytes"] --> netnew["g_mymalloc_netnewbytes"]
        g_mymalloc_netallocount["g_mymalloc_netallocount"] --> netcount["g_mymalloc_netnewcount"]
    end
```

**Memory Management Features**

The system provides two operational modes:

1. **Debug Mode** (`MYMALLOC_DBG=1`): Full allocation tracking with metadata
2. **Release Mode** (`MYMALLOC_DBG=0`): Minimal overhead wrapper

**Debug Mode Capabilities**:
- Per-allocation metadata with source file and line number
- Magic number corruption detection
- Linked list tracking of all active allocations
- Periodic memory usage summaries
- State dumping for leak analysis
- Memory access pattern tracing

Sources: [src/mymalloc.h:1-36](), [src/mymalloc_dbg.cpp:10-377]()

### Memory Debugging Interface

The debug memory system provides comprehensive tracking and analysis tools:

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Allocation Tracking"
        alloctrack["Allocation"] --> memdata["mem_data structure"]
        memdata --> magic["magic: 0x3e3e3e3e"]
        memdata --> srcinfo["fn:linenr"]
        memdata --> allocinfo["bytes, idx, secs"]
        memdata --> linkage["fwd/bwd pointers"]
    end
    
    subgraph "State Management"
        linkage --> blocklist["s_BlockList"]
        blocklist --> insert["InsertBlock()"]
        blocklist --> delete["DeleteBlock()"]
        insert --> summary["Summary Generation"]
        delete --> summary
    end
    
    subgraph "Reporting"
        summary --> mymalloc_print_summary["mymalloc_print_summary()"]
        summary --> mymalloc_write_state["mymalloc_write_state()"]
        summary --> mymalloc_write_map["mymalloc_write_map()"]
        summary --> tracing["Memory Tracing"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Periodic Operations"
        timer["Timer-based"] --> autosummary["Auto Summary"]
        timer --> autodump["Auto State Dump"]
        autosummary --> fd["File Descriptor I/O"]
        autodump --> fd
    end
```

**Memory Debugging Configuration**

The debug system supports runtime configuration through command-line options:
- `--myalloc_summary_secs`: Interval for periodic memory summaries
- `--myalloc_dump_secs`: One-time state dump after specified seconds
- `--myalloc_trace`: Enable per-allocation tracing
- `--myalloc_exit_state`: Generate state dump on application exit

Sources: [src/mymalloc_dbg.cpp:64-182](), [src/mymalloc_dbg.cpp:238-377]()

## Matrix and Memory Management

The application provides specialized matrix classes and memory management for dynamic programming operations.

### Matrix Class System

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Matrix Template"
        Mx["Mx<T>"] --> rowcount["m_RowCount"]
        Mx --> colcount["m_ColCount"]
        Mx --> data["m_Data**"]
        Mx --> buffer["m_Buffer*"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Memory Layout"
        buffer --> onebuffer["ONE_BUFFER mode"]
        onebuffer --> contiguous["Contiguous allocation"]
        contiguous --> rowpointers["Row pointer setup"]
        data --> rowpointers
    end
    
    subgraph "Operations"
        ops["Matrix Operations"] --> Alloc["Alloc(rows, cols)"]
        ops --> Get["Get(i, j)"]
        ops --> Put["Put(i, j, val)"]
        ops --> Assign["Assign(val)"]
        ops --> Clear["Clear()"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Specializations"
        XDPMem["XDPMem"] --> TBBit["m_TBBit: Mx<byte>"]
        XDPMem --> RevA["m_RevA: byte*"]
        XDPMem --> RevB["m_RevB: byte*"]
        XDPMem --> Buffer1["m_Buffer1: float*"]
        XDPMem --> Buffer2["m_Buffer2: float*"]
    end
```

**Matrix Implementation Details**

The `Mx<T>` template class provides:

- **Unified Memory Layout**: Single buffer allocation with computed row pointers for cache efficiency
- **Type Safety**: Template-based type checking for different data types
- **Bounds Checking**: Debug mode boundary validation
- **Resource Management**: Automatic cleanup in destructor

The `XDPMem` class extends this for dynamic programming:

- **Specialized Buffers**: Separate float and int buffers for different DP algorithms
- **Reverse Sequence Storage**: Buffers for reversed sequence data
- **Traceback Support**: Byte matrix for alignment path reconstruction
- **Offset Handling**: Buffer pointers adjusted for 1-based indexing

Sources: [src/mx.h:8-135](), [src/xdpmem.h:15-109]()

The codebase implements a comprehensive type system for cross-platform compatibility and performance optimization.

**Type System Design**

The type system provides:

- **Consistent Naming**: `uint32`, `uint64`, `byte` for clear intent
- **Platform Abstraction**: Compiler-specific `int64` definitions
- **Architecture Awareness**: `BITS` macro for 32/64-bit builds
- **Standard Compliance**: Proper constants and limits definitions

**Platform-Specific Adaptations**:
- **Windows**: `__int64`, `_stricmp`, `off_t` redefinition
- **GCC**: `long long`, `strcasecmp`, standard `off_t`
- **Debug Builds**: Unified `DEBUG` and `_DEBUG` macros

Sources: [src/myutils.h:4-104](), [src/myutils.h:141-143]()

## Purpose and Scope

This page documents the build system and continuous integration/continuous deployment (CI/CD) infrastructure for the reseek protein structure search tool. It covers the GitHub Actions workflows, cross-platform build processes, performance instrumentation, and artifact generation. For information about the core utilities and memory management systems that support the build process, see [Core Utilities and Memory Management](#8.2).

## Build System Overview

The reseek build system is designed for cross-platform compilation with automated CI/CD pipelines. The system supports multiple operating systems and architectures through platform-specific build scripts integrated with GitHub Actions workflows.

### CI/CD Pipeline Architecture

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "GitHub Actions"
        GH_TRIGGER["GitHub Trigger<br/>workflow_dispatch"]
        
        subgraph "macOS Build"
            OSX_WORKFLOW["build-osx-x86<br/>macos-13 runner"]
            OSX_DEPS["MacPorts + Homebrew<br/>python311, gcc@11"]
            OSX_BUILD["build_osx_x86.bash<br/>Platform Build Script"]
        end
        
        subgraph "Linux Build"  
            LINUX_WORKFLOW["build_linux_x86<br/>ubuntu-latest runner"]
            LINUX_DEPS["setup-python@v5<br/>Python 3.10"]
            LINUX_BUILD["build_linux_x86.bash<br/>Platform Build Script"]
        end
        
        subgraph "Artifact Management"
            OSX_ARTIFACT["reseek-osx-x86<br/>Binary Upload"]
            LINUX_ARTIFACT["reseek-linux-x86<br/>Binary Upload"]
        end
    end
    
    subgraph "Source Code"
        SRC_DIR["src/<br/>Source Directory"]
        BUILD_SCRIPTS["Platform Build Scripts<br/>*.bash"]
        GITIGNORE["Build Artifacts<br/>.gitignore"]
    end
    
    GH_TRIGGER --> OSX_WORKFLOW
    GH_TRIGGER --> LINUX_WORKFLOW
    
    OSX_WORKFLOW --> OSX_DEPS
    OSX_DEPS --> OSX_BUILD
    OSX_BUILD --> OSX_ARTIFACT
    
    LINUX_WORKFLOW --> LINUX_DEPS
    LINUX_DEPS --> LINUX_BUILD
    LINUX_BUILD --> LINUX_ARTIFACT
    
    SRC_DIR --> BUILD_SCRIPTS
    BUILD_SCRIPTS --> OSX_BUILD
    BUILD_SCRIPTS --> LINUX_BUILD
    
    GITIGNORE --> SRC_DIR
```

**Sources:** [.github/workflows/build_osx_x86.yml:1-35](), [.github/workflows/build_linux_x86.yml:1-37]()

## Platform-Specific Build Workflows

### macOS x86 Build Pipeline

The macOS build workflow `build-osx-x86` executes on `macos-13` runners and includes comprehensive dependency management:

| Component | Configuration |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Runner** | `macos-13` |
| **Package Managers** | MacPorts, Homebrew |
| **Dependencies** | `python311`, `gcc@11` |
| **Build Script** | `build_osx_x86.bash` |
| **Artifact** | `reseek-osx-x86` |

The workflow performs the following steps:
1. Repository checkout using `actions/checkout@v4`
2. MacPorts installation via `melusina-org/setup-macports@v1`
3. Dependency installation through both MacPorts and Homebrew
4. Execution of platform-specific build script
5. Binary artifact upload to `/Users/runner/work/reseek/reseek/bin/reseek`

### Linux x86 Build Pipeline

The Linux build workflow `build_linux_x86` provides a streamlined build process:

| Component | Configuration |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Runner** | `ubuntu-latest` |
| **Python Setup** | `actions/setup-python@v5` |
| **Python Version** | `3.10` |
| **Build Script** | `build_linux_x86.bash` |
| **Artifact** | `reseek-linux-x86` |

The workflow includes concurrency control with `cancel-in-progress: true` to prevent resource conflicts and features minimal permission requirements with `contents: read`.

**Sources:** [.github/workflows/build_osx_x86.yml:8-34](), [.github/workflows/build_linux_x86.yml:16-36]()

## Build Script Integration

### Build Script Execution Flow

```mermaid
graph LR
    subgraph "Workflow Trigger"

    CHECKOUT --> DEPS
    DEPS --> CHMOD
    CHMOD --> BASH_EXEC

```

The build scripts are platform-specific shell scripts located in the `src/` directory:
- `build_osx_x86.bash` - macOS x86 compilation
- `build_linux_x86.bash` - Linux x86 compilation

Both scripts are made executable using `chmod +x` before execution and operate within the `$GITHUB_WORKSPACE/src` directory context.

**Sources:** [.github/workflows/build_osx_x86.yml:24-28](), [.github/workflows/build_linux_x86.yml:26-30]()

### Timer Infrastructure

The build system includes comprehensive performance measurement capabilities through the timer infrastructure defined in `timers.h`. This system provides granular timing for various components of the build and runtime processes.

### Timer Categories

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Core Timers"
        T_NONE["None<br/>Default Timer"]
        T_OVERHEAD["GetTimerOverhead<br/>Timer Calibration"]
        T_TEST["TestTimer<br/>Timer Validation"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Memory Management"
        T_ALLOC["MxBase_Alloc<br/>Memory Allocation"]

        T_SORT["Sort<br/>Sorting Operations"]
        T_QUICKSORT["QuickSortInPlace<br/>In-place Sorting"]
        T_SW["SWFwd/SWRev<br/>Smith-Waterman"]
        T_ALIGN["DSS_Align1/2/3<br/>Alignment Phases"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Search Operations"
        T_SCORE["GetScorePosPair<br/>Score Calculation"]
        T_KMERS["SetKmersVec<br/>K-mer Processing"]
        T_PROFILES["SetProfiles<br/>Profile Generation"]
        T_EVALUE["CalcEvalue<br/>E-value Calculation"]
    end

    T_OVERHEAD --> T_TEST

    T_SCORE --> T_KMERS
    T_KMERS --> T_PROFILES
    T_PROFILES --> T_EVALUE
```

The timer system includes 60+ distinct timing categories covering:
- Core system operations (`GetTimerOverhead`, `TestTimer`)
- Memory management (`MxBase_Alloc`, `MxBase_AllocData`, `MxBase_FreeData`)
- Algorithm execution (`SWFwd`, `SWRev`, `DSS_Align1`, `DSS_Align2`, `DSS_Align3`)
- Search operations (`SetKmersVec`, `SetProfiles`, `CalcEvalue`)
- Sorting and data structures (`Sort`, `QuickSortInPlace`, `QuickSortOrder`)

**Sources:** [src/timers.h:1-61]()

```
make.stdout
make.stderr

vcxproj_make.py
```

These exclusions prevent build artifacts, log files, and generated configuration files from being committed to the repository.

### Manual Triggering

Both build workflows use `workflow_dispatch` triggers, requiring manual activation through the GitHub Actions interface. This approach provides controlled build execution for release management and testing purposes.

### Concurrency Management

The Linux build workflow implements concurrency control:
- **Group:** `${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}`
- **Cancel in Progress:** `true`

This configuration prevents multiple simultaneous builds on the same branch, optimizing resource usage and preventing conflicts.
